lede: To Spark, `"Senior Software Engineer"` and `"  senior software engineer"` are two different titles. Before you count, compare or join text, make every value follow one standard form.
objectives: Remove stray spaces with `trim` and inner runs of spaces with `regexp_replace`
Pick one case for text you compare, such as lower-case emails
Rewrite values like phone numbers into one format
Map known variants to one canonical value with `replace`, and split raw text lines safely

blocks.md:
The `employees` table comes from an HR system that people type into. Most values are tidy, but not all of them. Text comparisons in Spark are exact, so a leading space or a capital letter is enough to make two equal values look different.

**Standardizing** means choosing one form for a value and rewriting every row into it. The tools are the string functions you already know, applied with `select` and `alias`.

blocks.title: Trim the ends and lower the case
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

employees.select("employee_id", "job_title", "email").show(truncate=False)

employees.select(
    "employee_id",
    F.trim("job_title").alias("job_title"),
    F.lower("email").alias("email"),
).show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: `truncate=False` shows the two spaces in front of E0004's title. `trim` removes spaces at both ends, and `lower` makes E0007's email match the others. Email addresses aren't case sensitive, so lower case is the usual standard.

blocks.md:
`trim` only touches the ends. A value like `"Software  Engineer"`, with two spaces in the middle, needs a regular expression: `r"\s+"` matches one or more spaces, and `regexp_replace` turns each run into a single space.

When a value is only used to compare or group, such as a job title, a lower-case version is often the simplest standard. Call it a key so it's clear it isn't for display.

blocks.title: One space between words
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

titles = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("Software  Engineer",), ("  data manager ",), ("SENIOR   Data Analyst",)],
    "job_title STRING",
)

title_key = F.lower(F.regexp_replace(F.trim("job_title"), r"\s+", " "))

titles.select(
    "job_title",
    F.length("job_title").alias("length"),
    title_key.alias("title_key"),
    F.length(title_key).alias("key_length"),
).show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: Steps can be stored in a Python variable like `title_key` and used more than once. The lengths show what changed: every extra space is gone.

blocks.md:
Some values have a format, not just spacing. Phone numbers arrive as `555-201-3344`, `(555) 201-3344`, `555.201.3344`, `+1 555 201 3344` or `5552013344`. A reliable way to standardize them is:

1. Keep only the digits: `regexp_replace(phone, "[^0-9]", "")`. `[^0-9]` means any character that isn't a digit.
2. Keep the last ten digits, which drops a leading country code `1`. `F.substring(digits, -10, 10)` counts from the end.
3. Put the dashes back with groups: `r"(\d{3})"` captures three digits, and `$1` in the replacement puts them back.

blocks.title: Five phone formats, one result
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

phones = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("555-201-3344",), ("(555) 201-3344",), ("555.201.3344",), ("+1 555 201 3344",), ("5552013344",), (None,)],
    "phone STRING",
)

digits = F.regexp_replace("phone", "[^0-9]", "")
last_ten = F.substring(digits, -10, 10)
standard = F.regexp_replace(last_ten, r"^(\d{3})(\d{3})(\d{4})$", "$1-$2-$3")

phones.select("phone", digits.alias("digits"), standard.alias("standard")).show()
blocks.note: All five spellings end up as `555-201-3344`. A missing phone stays missing: string functions give NULL for NULL, so you don't need a special case.

blocks.md: Sometimes the variants are words, not spacing: `eng` and `Engineering` mean the same department. After trimming and lowering, list the known variants in a Python dict and let `replace` swap them. `subset` names the columns to touch; values that aren't in the dict stay as they are.

blocks.title: Map variants to one value
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

depts = spark.createDataFrame(
    [("E1", "Engineering"), ("E2", " eng"), ("E3", "ENGINEERING"), ("E4", "Fin "), ("E5", "finance")],
    "employee_id STRING, department STRING",
)

tidy = depts.select("employee_id", F.lower(F.trim("department")).alias("department"))
tidy.show()

tidy.replace({"eng": "engineering", "fin": "finance"}, subset=["department"]).show()
blocks.note: `replace` matches whole values only: it changes `eng` but would leave `engineer` alone. Trim and lower first, so the dict needs one entry per variant, not one per spelling.

blocks.md:
Raw exports are messier still. `employees_raw` is the same HR data as plain text lines, one `value` column, with `;` between fields. `F.split("value", ";")` turns each line into a list of fields, and `.getItem(i)` picks field `i`, counting from 0.

One line in the export is cut short. Watch what happens when you ask for a field it doesn't have.

blocks.title: A short line breaks getItem
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

parts = F.split("value", ";")
employees_raw.select(parts.getItem(0).alias("employee_id"), parts.getItem(3).alias("department")).show()
blocks.note: E0005's line has only three fields, so there is no field 3. Spark stops the whole job instead of guessing.

blocks.title: Read fields safely with get
blocks.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

lines = employees_raw.filter(F.col("value").rlike(r"^E\d"))
parts = F.split("value", ";")
lines.select(
    parts.getItem(0).alias("employee_id"),
    F.get(parts, 3).alias("department"),
    F.size(parts).alias("fields"),
).show(truncate=False)
blocks.note: Read as text, the file's header line is just another line, so `filter` keeps only the lines that start with an employee id. `F.get(parts, 3)` gives NULL when field 3 is missing, and `F.size` counts the fields. Two lines stand out: E0005 has 3 fields, and E0007 has 7 because its job title contains a `;` inside quotes. Splitting on `;` can't handle quotes; reading the file as CSV with `sep=";"` can.

concept.prompt: What does `F.trim` give for the value `"  data  manager "`?
concept.why: `trim` removes spaces at the two ends only. The two spaces in the middle stay; collapse them with `regexp_replace(..., r"\s+", " ")`.
It removes every character that isn't a digit, so the `+` and spaces go but the country code `1` stays. Keeping the last ten digits removes it.

concept.prompt: A raw line splits into 3 fields. What does `F.get(parts, 3)` give for it?
choices: An error that stops the job
concept.why: `F.get` gives NULL for a field that isn't there. `parts.getItem(3)` is the one that stops the job with an out-of-bounds error.

review: Text comparisons are exact: spaces and case make equal values look different.
`F.trim` removes spaces at both ends; `F.regexp_replace(col, r"\s+", " ")` turns inner runs of spaces into one.
Pick one case for values you compare, such as `F.lower` for emails and title keys.
For formats like phone numbers: keep the digits, keep the last ten, then rebuild the format with regex groups.
`df.replace(dict, subset=[...])` maps whole known variants to one canonical value.
`F.split` turns a raw line into fields; `F.get` gives NULL for a missing field where `getItem` stops the job.
